messages.subject: Optimizing Large RHadoop Jobs
messages.body_plain:
We have a very large data set in CSV, say 4-20 GB, and the data is organized by days. The days are very large data sets, say 1/5 of data per day, and we'd like to organize them into data frames for ease of use but I'm running into serialization issues on the java side. We've set the JVM max memory to around 3/4 GB yet it's still running out of memory serializing the data out of the reducers into HDFS.

Is there any guidance for the maximum number of distinct fields per data frame that can very serialized in a certain amount of memory? It's still not clear to me how RHadoop reads into memory and what is streamed as well as why the structures consume so much memory (perhaps a custom serialization format is in order ala Avro). Are all keys and values for a reducers loaded in at once or are they read only per key and written to HDFS before the next set is read? The challenge is that with really large data sets its very easy to not create distinct enough keys in the mapping phase causing too much to be loaded into memory on the reducer it seems. Without controls to force uniqueness and with R and Rhadoop seeming to load everything into memory it's easy to run OOM quickly.

It's also interesting trying to read any semblance of this data frame data from HDFS back to the local machine. Reading a 4GB result set back from reducer and into R memory using Rhadoop takes well over 4 hours (if it finishes at all)! Doing a copy of the data locally from HDFS only takes like 20-30 seconds so the rest is de serialization overhead. I thought it was a local java memory allocation setting or something but I can't seem to up the any there at all. Changing the output format to say CSV or even native but instead of data frames using just vectors takes 30 minutes to load into memory.

Any insight or best practices you can offer would be appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#948] Optimizing Large RHadoop Jobs
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jul 31, 2013 at 6:49 PM, Sean Willson <sean.w...@gmail.com> wrote:
> We have a very large data set in CSV, say 4-20 GB, and the data is organized by days. The days are very large data sets, say 1/5 of data per day, and we'd like to organize them into data frames for ease of use but I'm running into serialization issues on the java side. We've set the JVM max memory to around 3/4 GB yet it's still running out of memory serializing the data out of the reducers into HDFS.
>
> Is there any guidance for the maximum number of distinct fields per data frame that can very serialized in a certain amount of memory?

No.

> It's still not clear to me how RHadoop reads into memory

If you mean rmr2 and the mapreduce call specifically, the goal is to make it unnecessary for a user to know how features are implemented so you won't get a description of how it's done in the documentation, because if you have to do that then you have already lost as a developer. So the only way you have to understand it is read the source code. In fact, the function map.loop in the streaming.R file will give away the secret. reduce.loop is the equivalent for the reduce phase.

> and what is streamed as well as why the structures consume so much memory

They don't. You are assuming that you know the root cause of your problem, which will prevent you from making any progress. The problem you are reporting is normally related to spurious data being written to stdout by your code or some package you are loading. This breaks the java typedbytes parser and it runs out of memory. Sometimes it's just a package that's writing messages out to stdout that are not intercepted by sink. In one instance I managed to get a developer to fix that.

> Are all keys and values for a reducers loaded in at once or are they read only per key and written to HDFS before the next set is read?

Neither. A certain amount of data is read at once and all the keys contained therein are processed but the last, which is kept aside for the next read operation since there is no key termination marker other than reading a different key.

> The challenge is that with really large data sets

Your data sets are not really large unless you are writing from 1980. It's unclear why you'd be using hadoop for 20GB.

> its very easy to not create distinct enough keys in the mapping phase causing too much to be loaded into memory on the reducer it seems.

That is a potential problem. The alternatives always seemed worse than the current solution. Depending on the problem, you could use combiners or modify the key one way or another to pick them from a larger domain. For instance, if your keys are the days as you seem to suggest, it is a very bad idea to process 1/5 of your data in each reducer  and reduce call, the former because you are limiting your level of parallelism to 5, the second because you are going to run out of memory (R, not JVM). You could split the data arbitrarily within each day, or by day and hour, or add in minutes. How easy it is to change your algorithm to operate on these partial datasets is highly problem dependent, but it's the very essence of programming in the mapreduce model. You don't get all the data in memory at once, not 1/2 of it or 1/5. You get small, constant sized bits and you need to deal with that.

> Without controls to force uniqueness and with R and Rhadoop seeming to load everything into memory it's easy to run OOM quickly.

If you have a single key, that's going to happen but you have only yourself to blame.

>
> It's also interesting trying to read any semblance of this data frame data from HDFS back to the local machine. Reading a 4GB result set back from reducer and into R memory using Rhadoop takes well over 4 hours (if it finishes at all)! Doing a copy of the data locally from HDFS only takes like 20-30 seconds so the rest is de serialization overhead. I thought it was a local java memory allocation setting or something but I can't seem to up the any there at all. Changing the output format to say CSV or even native but instead of data frames using just vectors takes 30 minutes to load into memory.
>
> Any insight or best practices you can offer would be appreciated.

We seldom pushed from.dfs near those sizes so you may know more than I do at that end of the spectrum. As you said the problem seems to be with data.frames, particularly when creating very small ones.
If you run this test:

> system.time(from.dfs(to.dfs(keyval(NULL,data.frame(x = 1:10^6)))))
   user  system elapsed
  8.244   0.700   6.842

You see I can read and write a million rows (very simple of course) in 6 seconds. A key of NULL tells rmr2 to split the data in reasonable chunks. But if we specify different keys for each row

> system.time(from.dfs(to.dfs(keyval(1:10^5,data.frame(x = 1:10^5)))))
   user  system elapsed
 43.673  12.110  53.134

9 times slower on 1/10th of the data, which more or less is the difference between compiled code and interpreted code.
Once we made the decision to use R's own serialization for data frames to support all of their features (col names etc) we sometimes have to create small data frames because Java sees R data as raw bytes, so we need to serialize each group of data with the same key and then surround it with headers that will make it understandable to Java.
We plan to address this specific use case in the future, not because it seems very common but because it is surprising and breaks the abstraction. But no matter what we do, if you have a billion distinct keys, even with one record each, the reduce calls are interpreted and as such they take their sweet time

> system.time(sapply(1:10^6, identity))
   user  system elapsed
  2.034   0.021   2.054

Yes, R function calls take 2 microseconds each, no matter how little they do. And I am talking the simple ones, look at this

> system.time(sapply(1:10^5, data.frame))
   user  system elapsed
 37.607   0.026  37.627

The last resort here is the vectorized.reduce option to mapreduce which will call reduce on multiple groups at a time (different keys). I am not aware of anybody using that feature and to really take advantage of it you may have to write your own C extension (there is an example in collocations.R)

Antonio

My csv file has dfs.block.size is such that the file gets broken into 200 blocks. So, Job starts with 200 mappers.

}

{
library(randomForest)
Sys.setenv(HADOOP_HOME="/software/hadoop")

library(rhdfs)
hdfs.init()
rf <- randomForest(formula=LVal~.-UID, data=v, ntree=50, importance=TRUE)

hdfsMapReduceCall <- function (input, output) {
mapreduce(input=input,
output=output,
map = UIDPartitionMapper,

verbose=T,
backend.parameters = list(hadoop = list(D="mapred.reduce.tasks=6")))
}
hdfsMapReduceCall(hInputFile, hOutputFile)

Is my mapper correct?

In hInputFile, can I give path of HDFS folder (having all the same format files), and assume that even though my data is splitted across multiple files and each files further splitted in blocks by HDFS, mapper function will still get called for each line?
I was under an impression that one key is processed by a single reducer. But when I run the code, I can see that a single key is sent out to multiple reducers and then they are getting executed. I want to avoid that. I want that one key MUST get processed by a single reducer task only so the randomForest function is called only once for each UID, and has access to complete data associated to that UID.
Any other better way of creating a separate UID.rf file from my reducer?

We fixed that and everything was fine. But you need to do that kind of detailed analysis. Or you could do a few local runs using the debugger (see rmr.options, backend). In short, rmr2 or not you can not get away without debugging. You have to learn how to debug programs in hadoop. It's not me, you or rmr2, it's how programming is.

Antonio
